springdisc.name: Spring-applied, electromagnetically released disc brake
springdisc.role: Fail-safe: power off, the springs set the brake. The standard motor brake.
springdisc.body: A friction disc on the motor shaft is clamped between an armature plate and a fixed plate by springs. A DC coil, when energised, pulls the armature against the springs and frees the disc. Loss of power sets the brake, which is what makes it the holding brake on hoists and inclines. The air gap between armature and coil body is the adjustment; the disc thickness is the wear limit; the coil, rectifier, and voltage are the actuator.
tips: Air gap at three points, brake set, feeler gauge, against the nameplate nominal and maximum.
Rectifier and coil voltage checked before the mechanics are blamed for a brake that drags or will not release.
Manual release lever back to off.
Disc replaced at the minimum thickness; the armature and plate faces checked for scoring and flatness.

emclutch.name: Electromagnetic clutch (power-on engaged)
emclutch.role: Energise the coil to pull the armature onto the rotor and transmit torque. Packaging, indexing, small drives.
emclutch.body: A coil in a stationary field housing, a rotor on the input shaft, and an armature on the output. Energised, the armature snaps onto the rotor face and drives. De-energised, a spring or a leaf spring lifts it clear. Fast, clean, and low maintenance until the gap grows or the faces glaze. Tooth clutches (positive engagement) are the variant for indexing with no slip.
tips: Air gap between armature and rotor per the manual; too large and the coil cannot pull the armature across.
Faces glaze from slipping engagement; the coil voltage and the load inertia against the rating.
Bearings in the rotor and field assembly are the mechanical wear item.

airdisc.name: Air-actuated clutch and brake, and clutch-brake units
airdisc.role: A piston clamps the friction discs. High cycle rates, presses, and machines that must stop within a set angle.
airdisc.body: Air pressure on a piston engages the clutch; a spring or a second air chamber sets the brake. Combined clutch-brake units on presses connect the flywheel to the crank and stop the crank within a few degrees, hundreds of times an hour. The air supply (pressure, volume, dryness, and the control valve) is the actuator; friction discs and the mating surfaces are the wear; clearance is the adjustment. On a press, the clutch-brake is a safety-rated component with a dual valve and monitoring.
tips: Air pressure at the unit against the spec. A turned-down regulator is a slipping clutch.
Stopping time on a press is measured and is part of the safeguarding distance (Safeguarding module).
Dual air valves with monitoring on presses; a valve fault is a stop condition, not a reset.
Quick exhaust valves for a fast brake set; dry air or the valves stick.

drum.name: Drum and shoe brakes
drum.role: External shoes on a drum, spring set, released by a thruster or a solenoid. Cranes, hoists, mills.
drum.body: Two shoes clamp a drum on the motor or gearbox shaft. Springs set them; an electro-hydraulic thruster or a solenoid releases them. Big, tolerant, and adjustable, with the shoe clearance and the spring setting (braking torque) both adjustable. The thruster has its own oil and its own stroke to check. Drum condition (heat checking, scoring, out of round) is inspected.
tips: Equal shoe clearance both sides; unequal drags one shoe.
Braking torque set by the spring compression dimension per the manual, and verified with a holding test.
Thruster oil level and stroke; a thruster that does not complete its stroke leaves the brake partly set.
Drum surface: heat checking is the sign of too much energy per stop.

caliper.name: Caliper disc brakes
caliper.role: Pads clamp a disc from both sides. Spring-applied hydraulically released for holding; hydraulically applied for service braking.
caliper.body: One or more calipers on a large disc, on winches, conveyor drives, mills, and wind turbines. Spring-applied, hydraulically released calipers are fail-safe holding brakes; hydraulically applied ones are service brakes with a separate holding brake. Pad thickness, disc run-out and thickness, hydraulic pressure and leaks, and the release stroke are the checks. Multiple calipers share the load and are adjusted together.
tips: Pad wear limit and disc thickness minimum from the manual.
Disc run-out with an indicator; a warped disc drags on one side per revolution.
Hydraulic release pressure at the caliper; a leak is a brake that sets by itself.
All calipers on a disc set to the same clearance.

wet.name: Wet (oil-immersed) multi-plate clutches and brakes
wet.role: Stacks of plates in oil. High energy, long life, smooth engagement. Gearboxes and mobile equipment.
wet.body: Alternating friction and steel plates on splines, clamped by a piston, running in oil that cools them and carries away wear. The oil is part of the friction system: it must be the specified fluid with the right friction modifiers, or the clutch chatters, slips, or grabs. Wear shows as increasing piston travel and falling holding torque. Used in transmissions, planetary drives, and hydraulic winches.
tips: The specified oil only. The wrong oil is the most common wet clutch complaint.
Piston travel or clearance measured as the wear indicator.
Oil contamination (water, metal) shows as chatter; oil analysis.
Hot oil after heavy use is normal; oil that smells burnt is plates that have overheated.

torquelimit.name: Torque limiters (overload clutches)
torquelimit.role: Slip or disengage above a set torque to protect the drive from a jam.
torquelimit.body: Friction types slip and re-engage when the overload clears (and generate heat while slipping). Ball detent types disengage completely and must be reset. Shear pin types break a pin and are replaced. Set to a torque just above the normal maximum. The common misuse is turning the setting up to stop nuisance trips, which removes the protection, and then the gearbox or the chain breaks instead.
tips: Setting verified with a torque wrench or a known load; recorded.
Nuisance trips are a process problem (jams, overloads) to be solved, not a setting to be raised.
Friction limiters that slip repeatedly overheat and glaze; a limiter that has slipped needs inspecting.
A disengaged ball detent limiter must be reset by hand; it will not re-engage on its own.

oneway.name: One-way clutches and backstops
oneway.role: Free in one direction, locked in the other. Sprag, roller ramp, and cam types.
oneway.body: Sprags (figure-eight shaped elements) or rollers on ramps wedge between inner and outer races in one direction and free-wheel in the other. As a backstop on an inclined conveyor or elevator, the clutch is mounted so the drive turns it freely forward and it locks the instant the drive stops, holding the loaded belt against runback. As an indexing or overrunning clutch, the same element lets a driven shaft coast past a stopped driver.
tips: Direction of installation: a backstop fitted backward locks the drive on start. Check the arrow.
Lubrication: sprag clutches need clean oil or the specified grease; contamination stops the sprags rolling over.
Tested by stopping the loaded conveyor: no runback.
Not a lockout; the load is free when the drive train is opened.

start.q: What is the clutch or brake doing?
start.hint: Load supported and locked out before hands go near it.

options.label: Brake will not hold, or the load creeps
Brake drags: hot, smells, motor labouring
Brake or clutch will not release or engage
Chatter, squeal, or a bang on engagement
Gap over maximum, or lining at the limit
Oil or grease on the surface

r_worn.label: worn: adjust or reline
r_worn.text: A gap past maximum means the springs are extended and the clamping force is down.
r_worn.sub: Adjust to nominal if within the adjustment range; if the lining is at minimum, reline and set the gap. Holding test before return to service.
r_worn.prevent: Gap and lining thickness measured and recorded every PM; the trend sets the reline date.

r_contam.label: contaminated friction surface
r_contam.text: Oil on a dry friction surface cuts the friction to a fraction.
r_contam.sub: Find the source: the motor or gearbox shaft seal next to the brake, over-greased bearings, a hydraulic leak. Fix it. Clean or replace the lining (oil-soaked organic lining does not recover).
r_contam.prevent: Seal condition on the adjacent machine on the PM. Grease quantity on the bearings.

r_glaze.label: glazed lining
r_glaze.text: A hard shiny surface from overheating or light dragging.
r_glaze.sub: Light sanding restores it once. Find the heat: dragging (gap too small, actuator not fully releasing), or energy per stop above the rating (cycle rate, load, speed). If it glazes again, the cause is still there.
r_glaze.prevent: Gap at nominal; actuator checked; duty against the rating.

r_undersized.label: brake undersized for the load, or a second brake carrying it
r_undersized.text: Correct gap, good lining, clean, and it still creeps: it is being asked to hold more than it can, or on a dual-brake hoist the other brake has been carrying the load.
r_undersized.sub: Brake torque rating against the load torque with the required factor (hoists: typically 150 percent of rated load torque per brake). Spring setting on adjustable brakes. Test each brake alone on a dual system. If the load grew, the brake is re-rated or replaced.
r_undersized.prevent: Holding test on each brake independently on the inspection interval.

drag1.q: Does it release fully when energised (or pressurised)?

options.label: No, or slowly: check the actuator
Yes, but the gap is closed up
Yes, gap correct, manual release lever position?

r_gap_small.label: gap too small or uneven
r_gap_small.text: Too little clearance, or a cocked armature, drags on one side.
r_gap_small.sub: Three-point gap measurement. Adjust for equal gap, then nominal. Check the disc runs true and the mating plate is flat.

r_lever.label: manual release partly engaged
r_lever.text: A release lever or screw not fully returned holds the brake partly off, or partly on.
r_lever.sub: Return it to the off position per the manual. Check the lever has not been bent or jammed by a guard.
r_lever.prevent: Manual release position on the return-to-service checklist.

act2.label: coil, rectifier, or voltage
act2.text: A DC brake coil that does not get its voltage does not release; a weak one releases slowly and drags.
act2.sub: Voltage at the coil when energised against the nameplate (the electrician on the live check). Rectifier output. Coil resistance. Air gap too large for the coil to pull across. Wiring at the terminal box. Handoff package from the Motors module if it is electrical.
act2.prevent: Coil voltage and rectifier on the electrical PM. Gap within maximum.

r_air.label: air supply or valve
r_air.sub: Pressure at the unit under operation (not at the regulator). Quick exhaust valves sticking on wet air. Control valve shifting (Pneumatics module). Piston seals leaking. Air dryness.
r_air.prevent: Pressure at the unit recorded on the PM; air quality per the Pneumatics module.

r_hyd.label: thruster or hydraulic release
r_hyd.text: A thruster with low oil or a caliper with a leak does not complete its stroke.
r_hyd.sub: Thruster oil level and condition; stroke against the specification; the linkage free. Caliper: release pressure at the caliper, leaks, and the pump. A spring-applied caliper that sets by itself has lost hydraulic pressure.
r_hyd.prevent: Thruster oil and stroke on the PM. Hydraulic system on the Hydraulics module PM.

options.label: Torque limiter slipping under normal load

r_wet.label: wet clutch: oil, wear, or pressure
r_wet.text: Wet clutches slip on the wrong oil, worn plates, or low apply pressure.
r_wet.sub: Oil against the specification (friction modifiers matter). Piston travel or clearance as the wear indicator. Apply pressure at the piston. Oil analysis for contamination.
r_wet.prevent: Specified oil on the tag. Piston travel recorded.

r_noise.label: chatter, squeal, or bang
r_noise.text: Chatter is stick-slip on engagement: contamination, glazing, the wrong oil on a wet clutch, or a loose mounting. Squeal is a dry lining under light drag. A bang is excessive gap or a loose hub or key.
r_noise.sub: Surface condition and contamination. Gap. Hub, key, and mounting bolts. Wet clutch oil. Cycle rate and energy against the rating.
r_noise.prevent: Gap and mounting on the PM. Correct oil.

r_backstop.label: backstop or torque limiter
r_backstop.text: A backstop that lets the belt run back, or a torque limiter that slips at normal load or never slips at a jam.
r_backstop.sub: Backstop: direction of installation, lubrication (clean oil or the specified grease; contamination stops the sprags), and a runback test with the loaded conveyor. Torque limiter: the setting verified with a torque wrench; a friction limiter that has been slipping is glazed; a ball detent that tripped must be reset. A limiter turned up to stop nuisance trips has no protection: fix the jams.
r_backstop.prevent: Backstop runback test and limiter setting on the PM, recorded.

panels.overview:
A clutch connects, a brake stops, and both turn energy into heat through friction
A clutch transmits torque between a driver and a driven shaft on command; a brake absorbs the kinetic energy of a moving load and holds it stopped. Both use friction surfaces pressed together by a spring, air, oil, or a magnet, and both wear those surfaces at a rate set by the energy per engagement and the number of engagements. The three questions on any clutch or brake are: is the air gap or adjustment correct, is the friction material within wear limits, and is the actuator (spring, coil, cylinder) delivering the force it should. A brake that holds a suspended load is also a safety device and is treated as one.
Where they are and what they do
  • Motor brakes: a spring-applied, electrically released disc brake on the motor NDE. Power off, the brake sets; power on, the coil pulls the armature and releases it. Hoists, cranes, conveyors on inclines, indexers, anything that must stop and stay stopped.
  • Clutch-brake units: on presses, packaging machines, and indexers, a combined unit that connects the flywheel to the crank and stops the crank on demand, air or electrically actuated, cycling many times a minute.
  • Overload clutches: torque limiters that slip or disengage when the load exceeds a setting, protecting the drive from a jam. Ball detent, friction, and shear pin types.
  • Backstops: one-way clutches on inclined conveyors and elevators that let the drive turn forward and lock against reverse rotation when the drive stops.
  • Fluid couplings and soft-start clutches: let the motor start unloaded and pick the load up smoothly; the Couplings module covers the fluid coupling.
  • Centrifugal clutches: engage as speed rises; small engines and some fans.
Field tip: a brake that smells is a brake that is draggingThe smell of hot friction material from a motor brake with the motor running is a brake that has not fully released: the air gap is closed up by wear, the coil is weak or on the wrong voltage, or the rectifier has failed. It is eating itself and heating the motor, and when the lining is gone the load drops. Infrared on the brake housing on the PM; hotter than the motor is dragging.

panels.friction:
Friction material: the consumable that decides everything
  • Materials: organic (resin bonded fibre, the common one), sintered metallic (high energy, high temperature), and specialty (paper for wet clutches, ceramic). Asbestos was the fibre until the 1990s; old linings and old spare linings in stores are treated as asbestos until proven otherwise (Seals module Safety tab has the handling rule).
  • Energy per engagement: the kinetic energy of the load stopped, or the slip energy during clutch engagement, all becomes heat in the friction surfaces. Too much energy per stop, or too many stops per hour, overheats the material: it glazes, fades (loses friction when hot), cracks, or chars. The manufacturer rates the unit for energy per cycle and cycles per hour.
  • Wear limit: a minimum lining thickness, or a maximum air gap, on the nameplate or in the manual. Measured on the PM and replaced before the limit. A lining worn to the rivets or the backing plate scores the mating surface and the brake fails to hold.
  • Glazing: a shiny hard surface from overheating or from light dragging. Reduced friction, the brake slips or the clutch will not transmit. Light sanding restores it once; repeated glazing means the cause (dragging, overload) is still there.
  • Contamination: oil or grease on a dry friction surface cuts the friction to a fraction. A leaking shaft seal on the motor or gearbox next to a brake is a brake that will not hold. Wet clutches are the opposite: they need the specified oil, and the wrong oil (wrong friction modifier) makes them chatter or slip.
  • Mating surface: the disc, drum, or armature plate wears too. Scoring, heat checking (a network of fine cracks), bluing, and out-of-flat all reduce contact. Resurface or replace to the manufacturer limit.
  • Bedding in: new linings need a run-in at reduced load to seat to the mating surface; a new brake at full duty on day one glazes.
panels.adjust:
Adjustment and air gap
Every friction clutch and brake has a gap between the friction surfaces when disengaged, and that gap grows as the lining wears. Too large and a spring-applied brake has less spring force (the springs are less compressed) and a magnetic brake may not pull the armature across at all: the brake fails to release or, worse, fails to set fully. Too small and it drags. The manufacturer specifies a nominal gap and a maximum; adjustment brings it back to nominal, and when the adjustment range is used up the lining is replaced.
  • Electromagnetic disc brakes: air gap measured with a feeler gauge between the armature plate and the magnet body, at three or four points around the circumference, with the brake set (power off). Typical nominal 0.2 to 0.5 mm; maximum around 0.6 to 1.0 mm depending on size. Adjust with the sleeve nuts or the adjusting screws per the manual; equal gap all round.
  • Manual release levers on motor brakes: for moving a load by hand under controlled conditions; they must be returned to the released-off position or the brake is disabled.
  • Drum brakes: shoe clearance to the drum, equal on both shoes, set by the adjusting rods. Thruster or solenoid stroke checked so the brake fully releases at the end of the stroke and fully sets when de-energised.
  • Air clutch-brake units: air pressure at the unit against the specification (a regulator that has been turned down is a clutch that slips), clearance per the manual, and the quick-exhaust valves that give a fast set on the brake side.
  • Torque limiters: the slip torque setting, by the spring compression dimension or the manufacturer's torque chart, verified with a torque wrench or a known load. A limiter set high to stop nuisance trips is a drive with no protection.
  • After adjustment: a functional test. Release and set with the load blocked, then a controlled test with the load, then the gap rechecked after the first shift.
  • Record the gap and the lining thickness every PM; the trend is the wear rate and the replacement date.
Field tip: three feeler readings, not oneAn armature plate that measures 0.3 mm at one spot and 0.8 mm opposite is cocked, and it will drag on the tight side and be weak on the loose side. Measure at three or four points, adjust for equal gap, then set the nominal. A brake with a rectifier or a coil fault can show the same symptom as a bad gap; check the voltage at the coil before condemning the mechanics.
panels.holding:
Holding brakes and backstops: when the brake is the only thing between the load and the floor
A holding brake on a hoist, a lift, or an inclined conveyor is a safety device
It holds a suspended load with the power off, every night, with nobody watching. It is inspected, tested, and adjusted on a schedule as a safety device, and any work on it is done with the load lowered or mechanically supported. A holding brake is never adjusted, released, or opened with a load hanging on it. Cranes and hoists in Ontario fall under Regulation 851 section 51 and CSA B167; the brake is part of the inspection.
  • Holding test: with the load at rest and the brake set, the drive is commanded (or the load is applied) and the brake must hold without creep. Some hoists have a brake test mode; others are tested with a rated test load. The manual sets the method and the interval.
  • Dual brakes: many hoists have a motor brake and a second load brake (a mechanical load brake in the gear train, or a second disc brake). Each is tested on its own; a hoist that holds on two brakes is not proving either one.
  • Backstops: sprag or roller ramp one-way clutches on the reducer or the head shaft of an inclined conveyor. They allow forward rotation and lock against reverse. Inspected for oil condition (some run in the gearbox oil, some are grease packed), for the correct direction of installation (a backstop fitted backward locks the drive), and tested by stopping the loaded conveyor and watching for runback.
  • A backstop is not a lockout. It holds the load against runback while the drive train is intact. Open the coupling or the gearbox and the load is free. Block the load before drive work.
  • Brake release for maintenance: the manual release lever or a screw on the brake lets the load be lowered under control. It is used with the load supported or the descent controlled, and it is returned to normal before the machine is released.
  • Coil voltage and rectifier: a DC brake coil fed through a rectifier from AC. A failed rectifier or low voltage is a brake that releases slowly or not at all, drags, and overheats.
panels.troubleshoot:
Clutch and brake fault diagnosis

Load supported, locked out. Then: air gap or clearance at three points against the specification. Lining thickness against the minimum. Mating surface condition. Contamination (oil, water). Manual release lever position. Then the actuator: coil voltage and rectifier, air pressure at the unit, spring condition, thruster stroke.

Running (from a safe position): smell and infrared for dragging; noise on engagement (chatter, squeal, bang); time to stop or to engage; creep with the brake set.

The three questions resolve almost all of it. A brake or clutch with correct gap, good lining, and a working actuator that still misbehaves is being asked for more energy than it is rated for.
panels.selfcheck:
Self-check: one question at a time, tap an answer, read why
Questions are grouped by the tab they test. Get one wrong and the correct answer lights up green with a one-line reason; use the link to reopen the tab and read it again. For a training program, a pass is every section answered and the reasons read, not a percentage.
panels.safety:
Safety: the load, the springs, and the heat
Releasing a brake releases whatever it was holding
A brake is opened, adjusted, or released only when the load it holds is lowered to rest or supported by something that does not depend on the brake. A spring-applied brake has compressed springs inside it that unload when the cover comes off. A clutch that engages unexpectedly connects a running motor to whatever your hands are near. Lockout, load control, and spring energy every time.
  • Suspended loads: lowered, cribbed, or pinned before brake work. Hoists and cranes: the manufacturer's procedure and Regulation 851 section 51.
  • Spring energy: brake springs are compressed in the assembly. Disassembly per the manual, with the compression released in a controlled way (a press, or the adjusting screws backed off in sequence). Springs that let go are projectiles.
  • Electrical: the brake coil and rectifier are on the motor supply or a separate circuit. Lockout covers both. A brake coil is a DC circuit that can hold a charge in a large coil for a moment after switch-off.
  • Air clutch-brake units: the air is stored energy. Isolate and vent; the quick exhaust valves do not vent the supply side.
  • Heat: a brake after a heavy stop or a dragging brake is hot enough to burn. Infrared before hands.
  • Friction dust: old linings may be asbestos. Wet cleaning, no compressed air, and the asbestos procedure for anything unknown. Modern linings still produce dust that should not be breathed.
  • Manual release levers returned to the off position before the machine is handed back. A brake left released is a load that drops on the first stop.
  • Test with the load: after any brake work, a holding test and a controlled stop test before the machine returns to service, with nobody under the load.
